title: Sukuk
excerpt: Islamic investment certificates. Instead of lending money and collecting interest (which is riba), sukuk holders own a share of a real asset or project — like a
text: Islamic investment certificates. Instead of lending money and collecting interest (which is riba), sukuk holders own a share of a real asset or project — like an airport terminal — and earn returns from the profit it generates. Often called 'Islamic bonds,' but they are ownership certificates, not debt.

title: Islamic ETFs and Shariah stock screening
excerpt: How an ETF holding Apple or Microsoft can be halal: the fund tracks an index of stocks screened against Islamic rules — no interest-based income, no alcohol, ga
text: How an ETF holding Apple or Microsoft can be halal: the fund tracks an index of stocks screened against Islamic rules — no interest-based income, no alcohol, gambling or arms businesses, and strict limits on debt. A Shariah board certifies compliance, and any small leftover non-compliant income is 'purified' by donating it to charity.

title: Private credit
excerpt: Loans made directly to companies by non-bank lenders (like investment funds) instead of through a bank. It has been one of the fastest-growing corners of conven
text: Loans made directly to companies by non-bank lenders (like investment funds) instead of through a bank. It has been one of the fastest-growing corners of conventional finance; Shariah-compliant versions structure the lending without interest — for example through cost-plus sales or profit-sharing deals.

title: Murabaha
excerpt: A 'cost-plus' sale used across Islamic finance. The bank buys an asset (a house, car, or machine) and sells it to the customer at a disclosed price — its cost p
text: A 'cost-plus' sale used across Islamic finance. The bank buys an asset (a house, car, or machine) and sells it to the customer at a disclosed price — its cost plus an agreed profit markup — paid in fixed installments. Because the bank genuinely buys and then sells the asset, this counts as trade rather than an interest-bearing loan. Example: halal home financing, where the bank buys a house and resells it to the buyer at a fixed marked-up price paid over years.

title: Additional Tier 1 (AT1) sukuk
excerpt: A type of bank funding that sits between equity and ordinary debt: it can absorb losses if the bank gets into trouble, and the bank can usually redeem (call) it
text: A type of bank funding that sits between equity and ordinary debt: it can absorb losses if the bank gets into trouble, and the bank can usually redeem (call) it on a set date. Dubai Islamic Bank's $500 million AT1 sukuk, issued in 2021, is the Shariah-compliant version of this instrument — called on its first call date, October 19, 2026.

title: Short interest
excerpt: The total number of a stock's (or ETF's) shares that investors have borrowed and sold, betting the price will fall. A rise in short interest means more traders
text: The total number of a stock's (or ETF's) shares that investors have borrowed and sold, betting the price will fall. A rise in short interest means more traders are taking that side of the bet. Example: short interest in Wahed's HLAL halal ETF jumped 66% during September 2026 — though at under 1% of shares, it was still a small position.
